title: 1 Kings 4:20–34
context: The chapter closes with a summary of Solomon’s prosperity and wisdom. Judah and Israel are as numerous as the sand by the sea, the kingdom enjoys peace and abundant provision, and Solomon’s dominion extends widely. The narrator then celebrates his God-given wisdom, which surpasses that of the east and of Egypt and expresses itself in proverbs, songs, and observations of the natural world. In English Bibles, including the WEB, these verses are numbered 4:20–34; in the Hebrew text, 4:21–34 corresponds to 5:1–14, so chapter 5 in Hebrew begins with what English Bibles number 4:21. The engwebp edition used here follows the English numbering, running chapter 4 through verse 34. Details such as the exact extent of Solomon’s rule and the number of horse stalls (compare 2 Chronicles 9:25) are read differently by interpreters. Both traditions see this passage as a picture of God’s promises flourishing, while the narrator’s later account will show how that flourishing was put at risk.

verses.text: Judah and Israel were numerous as the sand which is by the sea in multitude, eating and drinking and making merry.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Judah and Israel are described as numerous as the sand by the sea, eating, drinking, and rejoicing. Many see an echo of God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17), now visible in a time of peace and plenty, and they observe that such blessing called for grateful faithfulness from the people who enjoyed it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see in this verse the fulfillment of God’s covenant promises to the patriarchs, displayed in the abundance of Solomon’s reign. Both traditions agree that the image of eating, drinking, and celebrating portrays the goodness of life under God’s blessing, and that the narrator presents it as the fruit of God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the River to the land of the Philistines, and to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon ruled over kingdoms from the River to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt, receiving tribute. Many connect this with the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18), though interpreters differ on how far this rule extended in practice and whether it describes direct control or a looser network of tribute.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see this verse as recalling the boundaries promised to Abraham, now reflected in Solomon’s reign. Both traditions agree that the narrator presents the wide reach of Solomon’s influence as a sign of God’s blessing, while acknowledging uncertainty about the exact political arrangements involved in this summary.

verses.text: Solomon’s provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour, sixty measures of meal,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon’s daily provision included thirty cors of fine flour and sixty measures of meal. The quantities describe the scale of the royal court and its many dependents, and they invite reflection on both the abundance of the kingdom and the cost borne by the people who supplied it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the figures as illustrating the wealth and size of Solomon’s court. Both traditions agree that the narrator records these amounts to show the prosperity of the reign, and both note that the demands of maintaining such a court would later become part of the burden the people felt.

verses.text: ten head of fat cattle, twenty head of cattle out of the pastures, and one hundred sheep, in addition to deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the provision included cattle, sheep, and various game, showing the richness of the royal table. The detail emphasizes abundance, yet it also connects with the later warnings about royal excess, inviting readers to consider how blessing can become a temptation when wealth is not held with humility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list of meats as a picture of plenty, while recognizing that the narrator’s later account will judge Solomon’s heart. Both traditions agree that the verse describes real abundance as part of God’s blessing, and that the way such abundance is used becomes an important theme in the story of Solomon.

verses.text: For he had dominion over all on this side of the River, from Tiphsah even to Gaza, over all the kings on this side of the River; and he had peace on all sides around him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon had dominion from Tiphsah to Gaza and enjoyed peace on all sides. Peace is presented as one of the great blessings of his reign, fitting the meaning often associated with his name, and Arminian interpreters observe that such peace provided an opportunity for faithful worship and building.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the peace on all sides as a fulfillment of God’s promise of rest for his people (compare 2 Samuel 7:10–11). Both traditions agree that the extent of Solomon’s dominion is presented as a summary of God’s blessing, while interpreters differ on how literally to take its geographical scope.

verses.text: Judah and Israel lived safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Judah and Israel lived safely, every man under his vine and fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba. The image portrays security and contentment in ordinary life, and later prophets use similar language for the peace God promises (Micah 4:4), showing that this picture became a lasting symbol of hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the vine and fig tree as an image of covenant blessing and peace that the prophets would later use to describe God’s future kingdom. Both traditions agree that the verse portrays an ideal of rest and safety that God gave in Solomon’s day and that points beyond it to a fuller peace.

verses.text: Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses and twelve thousand horsemen. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 9:25 gives four thousand stalls, and interpreters explain the difference in various ways, including possible copying variation; many also recall the warning against kings multiplying horses (Deuteronomy 17:16).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the numerical difference with Chronicles and treat it carefully rather than forcing a single explanation. Both traditions agree that the verse shows the military strength of Solomon’s kingdom, and both observe that the buildup of horses sits uneasily beside the law’s warning about royal reliance on military power.

verses.text: Those officers provided food for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon’s table, every man in his month. They let nothing be lacking.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the district officers provided food for the king and all who ate at his table, letting nothing be lacking. The verse shows the system of chapter 4 working as intended, with faithful officers fulfilling their responsibilities, and it highlights how the kingdom’s prosperity depended on many people doing their part.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the verse as evidence of the orderly provision God granted through Solomon’s administration. Both traditions agree that the statement that nothing was lacking portrays the abundance of the kingdom, while the scale of the royal table also hints at the demands placed on the people.

verses.text: They also brought barley and straw for the horses and swift steeds to the place where the officers were, each man according to his duty.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the officers also brought barley and straw for the horses and swift steeds, each according to his duty. The detail completes the picture of a well-supplied kingdom, and it reinforces the theme of faithful service by officers who carried out their assigned tasks.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the verse as part of the description of an ordered and prosperous administration. Both traditions agree that the provision for horses connects with the earlier mention of Solomon’s chariots, and that the narrator presents the system as functioning well in this season of the kingdom’s life.

verses.text: God gave Solomon abundant wisdom, understanding, and breadth of mind like the sand that is on the seashore.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers emphasize that God gave Solomon abundant wisdom, understanding, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore. The image echoes the description of the people in verse 20, and Arminian interpreters note that this gift, though great, still called for Solomon’s ongoing faithfulness to use it well.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the verse explicitly names God as the giver of Solomon’s wisdom, confirming the promise made at Gibeon. Both traditions agree that wisdom here is a divine gift rather than a human achievement, and that its abundance is meant to show the generosity of the God who answered Solomon’s request.

verses.text: Solomon’s wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon’s wisdom excelled that of the children of the east and of Egypt, regions known in the ancient world for wisdom traditions. The comparison places Israel’s king among the wise of the nations and suggests that God’s gift enabled him to surpass the best that surrounding cultures had produced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the comparison as showing the superiority of wisdom that comes from God. Both traditions agree that the verse honors the existence of wisdom among other peoples while presenting Solomon’s God-given wisdom as greater, and that the narrator’s point is to magnify the God who gave it.

verses.text: For he was wiser than all men—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol; and his fame was in all the nations all around.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon was wiser than all men, including Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol, and Darda. These names were evidently known for wisdom, and some may be connected with figures mentioned elsewhere (compare Psalms 88 and 89 titles; 1 Chronicles 2:6), though the relationships are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list of wise men as emphasizing the surpassing greatness of Solomon’s wisdom. Both traditions agree that the identification of these individuals is not fully certain, and that the verse’s main point is that Solomon’s fame spread among the nations because of the wisdom God had given him.

verses.text: He spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered one thousand five.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs and that his songs numbered one thousand five. The verse shows the breadth of his wisdom expressed in teaching and song, and while the book of Proverbs preserves some sayings associated with Solomon, the full collection mentioned here has not survived.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the large numbers as illustrating the richness of Solomon’s gift. Both traditions agree that the verse connects Solomon with the wisdom literature of Israel, and that the narrator presents his proverbs and songs as overflowing expressions of the wisdom God gave him.

verses.text: He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; he also spoke of animals, of birds, of creeping things, and of fish.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon spoke of trees, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop on the wall, and of animals, birds, creeping things, and fish. His wisdom included careful observation of creation, and Arminian interpreters see in this a recognition that studying the natural world is part of honoring the Creator.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see Solomon’s interest in creation as reflecting the order God built into the world, echoing the categories of creation in Genesis 1. Both traditions agree that wisdom in Scripture includes attention to the created order, and that the verse affirms the goodness of understanding the world God made.

verses.text: People of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, sent by all kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that people from all nations came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, sent by kings who had heard of it. The verse anticipates the visit of the queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1–9) and shows the international reach of the blessing God gave Israel, drawing the nations toward the wisdom of Israel’s king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the gathering of the nations as a sign of God’s purpose to bless the world through his people. Both traditions agree that the verse presents Solomon’s wisdom as a light to the nations in this period, and that the narrator’s praise sets the stage for the later account of how Solomon’s heart turned away.
